summary.title: Metal-Free Photocatalysis at Charged Aqueous Interface: Boosting the Photocatalytic Oxidative Coupling of Arylamines to Azoaromatics under Ambient Conditions †
summary.authors: Shivendra Singh; Vidhi Agarwal; Tridib K Sarma; Tushar Kanti Mukherjee
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a sustainable, metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling (POC) of arylamines to azoaromatics at charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles. The method utilizes Eosin Y (EY) as a low-cost organic photocatalyst and CTAB micelles as a scaffold to facilitate non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET). Under ambient air atmosphere and green light irradiation, the reaction achieves 100% conversion and selectivity within 4 hours using only 0.6 mol% photocatalyst. This approach significantly outperforms previous methodologies, which often suffered from slow kinetics, poor selectivity, high catalyst doses, or the need for inert atmospheres and organic solvents. The micellar environment modulates redox potentials and brings the photocatalyst and substrates into close proximity, enabling ultrafast PET with a time constant of 0.3 ps. The reaction mechanism involves the oxidation of arylamines by excited EY, followed by radical coupling and regeneration of the photocatalyst via reduction of atmospheric oxygen to hydrogen peroxide. The method demonstrates a broad substrate scope, including electron-rich and electron-deficient arylamines, and offers a green, aqueous-phase alternative for the synthesis of important azoaromatic compounds used in optical storage and molecular switches.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a sustainable, metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling (POC) of arylamines to azoaromatics at charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles. The method utilizes Eosin Y (EY) as a low-cost organic photocatalyst and CTAB micelles as a scaffold to facilitate non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET). Under ambient air atmosphere and green light irradiation, the reaction achieves 100% conversion and selectivity within 4 hours using only 0.6 mol% photocatalyst. This approach significantly outperforms previous methodologies, which often suffered from slow kinetics, poor selectivity, high catalyst doses, or the need for inert atmospheres and organic solvents. The micellar environment modulates redox potentials and brings the photocatalyst and substrates into close proximity, enabling ultrafast PET with a time constant of 0.3 ps. The reaction mechanism involves the oxidation of arylamines by excited EY, followed by radical coupling and regeneration of the photocatalyst via reduction of atmospheric oxygen to hydrogen peroxide. The method demonstrates a broad substrate scope, including electron-rich and electron-deficient arylamines, and offers a green, aqueous-phase alternative for the synthesis of important azoaromatic compounds used in optical storage and molecular switches.

Research Context
Azoaromatics are important functional organic molecules with applications in optical storage and molecular switches. Traditional diazotization methods produce unstable diazonium intermediates and unwanted waste. Metal nanoparticle-catalyzed syntheses often suffer from slow kinetics and poor selectivity. Photocatalytic reductive coupling of nitrobenzenes suffers from poor product selectivity. Previous photocatalytic oxidative coupling methods using Ir-based catalysts suffer from slow kinetics and high catalyst dose. Earlier reports utilized organic solvents due to low solubility of amine substrates in water. Designing an efficient green catalytic route in aqueous medium is of great importance.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to formulate a highly efficient POC methodology for azo compounds at charged aqueous interfaces. The hypothesis is that micellar surfaces act as efficient scaffolds to host photocatalyst and substrates. It is predicted that this setup enables non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer. The approach is expected to show fast kinetics and broad substrate scope. The method aims to outperform previously reported catalytic methodologies. The boosting of catalytic efficacy is attributed to non-diffusive PET and redox potential modulation.

Methodological Details
The study utilized Eosin Y (EY) as the photocatalyst and CTAB micelles as the interface. Photophysical behavior of EY was studied in the presence of CTAB, SDS, and TX-100. EY exhibited a bathochromic shift in the presence of CTAB and TX-100 micelles. EY showed enhanced fluorescence only in the presence of CTAB near the CMC. The fluorescence lifetime of EY increased from 1.17 ns in water to 2.74 ns in CTAB micelles. K3PO4 was used as the base in the reaction mixture. The reaction was triggered by green light at 525 nm under ambient air. The optimized reaction used 0.6 mol% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB. CTAB forms spherical micelles at an optimized concentration of 40 mM. Products were isolated and characterized using GC-MS and NMR measurements.

Procedures And Architectures
The reaction was optimized for the conversion of p-anisidine to 1,2-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene. The reaction achieved 100% conversion to the desired azo product within 4 hours. The reaction was feasible only in the presence of a base for proton abstraction. Both inorganic and organic bases were effective, with inorganic bases showing slightly higher yields. Atmospheric oxygen acts as a sacrificial oxidant for photocatalyst regeneration. Hydrogen peroxide formation was detected using H2O2 sensing strips. Fluorescence quenching experiments validated the PET phenomenon with a Stern-Volmer plot. The quenching rate constant was determined to be 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1. Fluorescence up-conversion measurements revealed an ultrafast PET time constant of 0.3 ps. Radical trap experiments using BHT validated the formation of amine radicals.

Key Results
The reaction achieved 100% conversion and 100% selectivity under ambient conditions. The method required only 0.6 mol% of photocatalyst, an 8.3-fold lower dose than previous reports. Electron-rich arylamines showed 100% conversion within 4 hours. Aniline as a substrate also showed 100% conversion under standard conditions. p-Chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline showed conversion yields of 98% and 95%, respectively. The quenching rate constant for p-anisidine was 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1. The PET time constant was measured at 0.3 ps. Radical trapping with BHT resulted in negligible conversion (~5.0%) to the azo product. A characteristic HR-MS peak for p-anisidine-BHT adducts appeared at 342.2399 g/mol.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The micellar surface acts as an efficient scaffold for non-diffusive PET. The interfacial surface charges dictate the interaction with charged molecules. The modulation of redox potentials at the CAI boosts catalytic efficacy. The method provides a green, aqueous-phase synthesis route for azoaromatics. This work opens new opportunities in the synthesis of azoaromatics.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a preprint and has not been peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv. The study focuses on specific substrates and may not cover all possible arylamine variants. The reaction requires specific micellar conditions and base for optimal performance.

Claims
The micellar interface enables ultrafast non-diffusive PET, significantly boosting reaction kinetics compared to bulk solution. Fluorescence up-conversion measurements reveal an ultrafast PET with a time constant of 0.3 ps. The quenching rate constant suggests a non-diffusive bimolecular quenching process.  This mechanism explains the high efficiency and fast reaction time of 4 hours.
The method is superior to previous Ir-based photocatalytic methods in terms of catalyst dose and reaction time. The method uses an 8.3-fold lower dose of EY compared to previous reports. The reaction completes in 4 hours, whereas previous methods took 24 hours.  This makes the process more sustainable and cost-effective.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Control experiments confirmed the formation of hydrogen peroxide via reduction of aerial oxygen. Radical trap experiments with BHT confirmed the involvement of amine radicals. The reaction was tested with various bases, showing inorganic bases were slightly more effective.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the photophysical behavior of EY in different micellar environments. Table 1 details the optimization of reaction conditions. Scheme 2a illustrates the broad substrate scope of the reaction. Figure 2 presents fluorescence quenching and up-conversion data.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a metal-free, aqueous-phase photocatalytic method for azoaromatic synthesis. 2. The strongest evidence is the 100% conversion and selectivity with ultrafast PET kinetics. 3. The future path involves expanding the substrate scope and scaling up the process.
